last_run: Close Call now shows the listed bid and ask of the same spreads next to the practice price, the break-even odds at the ask, and flags quotes too wide to trade.
next: Thursday: check the first Close Call questions (closing Wed Nov 18) graded right, and the new bid/ask box during market hours. Then the next finishing touch for Prof Brown's review.

replies.body: Close Call only said its practice prices were 'before bid/ask costs'. Tonight SPY's $725 YES practiced at $63 while the listed spread's ask was $105, more than the $100 it can pay, and a professor checking against his own screen would see neither number. Close Call now shows the listed bid and ask for the same YES and NO spreads beside the practice price, the odds you'd need to break even if you paid the ask, the cost of a round trip, and an amber note when the quotes are too wide to trade (usual outside market hours). Information only: odds, practice prices and grading unchanged.

The brain's Close Call record was only a summary, and its lean just nudges the market's odds by a few points, so 'right X% of the time' mostly repeats the market. A professor would want to see the actual calls and the few where the brain disagreed. Close Call now lists the brain's latest questions with both sets of odds, the close and right/wrong, marks the ones where it took the other side, and (once graded) how often those were right. First grades land Thursday. Information only: odds and grading unchanged.

Tonight every card on Moving now was red (Accenture 'story helps' at -3.4%, Microsoft -2.4%) with no word that the whole market fell, so you couldn't tell the story's effect from the market's. Each card now shows the S&P 500's move for the day at the top and each stock's move against it (for example -3.4 pts vs S&P). Only compared when both moves are from the same trading day. Information only: picks, grading and prices unchanged.

90-day results have fat tails: 81 graded calls moved more than 100% (one +508%), and one such call moves a 2,700-call test by about 0.2 pts. Nothing said whether a lead was broad or a few lottery tickets, which is the first thing a finance professor checks. Each research result now also reports the lead with results capped at the 1% extremes, the median call's lead and the 10 best calls' share, and the Brain page says it in one paragraph. Reporting only: the gate and the live ranking are unchanged.

Close Call's answer list said only 'right' or 'wrong', and a practice trade looked the same as 'Just call it'. But a YES trade (a call spread) that closes between its two strikes is right on the question and can still lose money, and the reverse for NO, so the page could say 'right' next to a trade that lost. Each traded answer now shows what's at risk, then what it made or lost at expiration, with a note when that differs from right/wrong, plus a 'Your practice trades' total that matches Portfolio. Information only: odds, pricing and grading unchanged.

Close Call asked 'Will NVDA close above $160 on Fri Nov 20?' with 40% odds, but those odds came from options priced for 130% volatility (NVDA has moved about 45% a year lately): the market expects a big earnings-week jump, and the page never said so. Now a 'How far it could move' box shows the range options give a 2-in-3 chance (a bar with today's price and your line), and an amber note when options expect a much bigger move than usual, often earnings or news before that date. Information only: the odds, the brain's lean and the trade prices are unchanged.

The Brain page's live forward test said the #1 pick's +0.4 pts lead was 'unlikely to be luck (t 2.1)', counting all 1,409 calls as independent. But they were made on only 14 days, and calls made the same week ride the same market, which the scorecard right above already counts honestly. The forward test now does the same: t 2.0 counted that way (still just clear of luck), with a line saying the calls came from 14 days and what the plain t was. The High/Medium/Low split uses the same check.

The Brain page's live forward test said '+0.4 pts on 1,409 calls', and right under it High -0.1, Medium -0.4, Low +0.6 pts on only 190 calls, with no word that the split is a smaller, newer sample. A professor would ask why the parts don't add up to the whole. It now says confidence labels began Nov 8, so the split covers only those 190 calls (together 0.0 pts vs +0.4 on all 1,409), and that no group is clear of luck yet.

Found a money bug in practice options: an expired trade (every Close Call practice trade) settled at whatever the stock was worth when you next opened Portfolio, not at the expiration-day close. On expiration morning it settled at the 10am price; a week later, at that week's price. So a Close Call YES that was right at Friday's close could show as a total loss on Monday. Now it settles at the official close on expiration day; until that close is in, Portfolio shows the trade as 'Settling' with an estimate, and it can't be closed by hand at an after-hours price.

A practice gain on its own says little: +$300 when the market rose 5% on the same money is worse than buying the index, and a finance professor judges every portfolio against a benchmark. Portfolio now has a 'You vs the S&P 500' card (your trades +$X, same money in the S&P 500 +$Y, ahead/behind by $Z, N of M beat the index) and each trade shows its own S&P line. Measured close to close in New York time, no look-ahead; the card says how.
